## Introduction

In this homework, I will explore the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset. I will clean the data, look at summary statistics and prepare it for regression modeling.

## Part 1: Reading the Data

### Loading Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(rsample)
```

### Reading the Dataset

The dataset contains hourly bike rentals and weather information from Seoul.

```{r}
bike_data <- read_csv(
  "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "Latin1")
)

head(bike_data)
dim(bike_data)
```

The dataset has 8,760 rows and 14 columns.

## Part 2: Exploratory Data Analysis

### Checking Missing Values

First, I checked whether the dataset contains any missing values.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(bike_data))
```

There are no missing values in the dataset.

### Checking Column Types

I checked the data types and summary statistics to understand the variables.

```{r}
str(bike_data)

bike_data |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  summary()
```

### Checking Categorical Variables

I checked the values in the categorical columns.

```{r}
unique(bike_data$Seasons)
unique(bike_data$Holiday)
unique(bike_data$`Functioning Day`)
```

### Converting Date

The Date column was stored as text, so I converted it into a date format.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  mutate(Date = dmy(Date))

head(bike_data$Date)
```

### Converting Categorical Variables

I converted the categorical variables into factors.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  mutate(
    Seasons = as.factor(Seasons),
    Holiday = as.factor(Holiday),
    `Functioning Day` = as.factor(`Functioning Day`)
  )

str(bike_data)
```

### Renaming Columns

I renamed the variables using lower snake case to make them easier to use.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  rename_with(~ "date", .cols = Date) |>
  rename_with(~ "bike_count", .cols = `Rented Bike Count`) |>
  rename_with(~ "hour", .cols = Hour) |>
  rename_with(~ "temp", .cols = starts_with("Temperature")) |>
  rename_with(~ "humidity", .cols = starts_with("Humidity")) |>
  rename_with(~ "wind_speed", .cols = starts_with("Wind speed")) |>
  rename_with(~ "visibility", .cols = starts_with("Visibility")) |>
  rename_with(~ "dew_point_temp", .cols = starts_with("Dew point")) |>
  rename_with(~ "solar_radiation", .cols = starts_with("Solar Radiation")) |>
  rename_with(~ "rainfall", .cols = starts_with("Rainfall")) |>
  rename_with(~ "snowfall", .cols = starts_with("Snowfall")) |>
  rename_with(~ "seasons", .cols = Seasons) |>
  rename_with(~ "holiday", .cols = Holiday) |>
  rename_with(~ "functioning_day", .cols = `Functioning Day`)

names(bike_data)
```

### Summary Statistics

I calculated the mean, median, minimum, and maximum number of bike rentals.

```{r}
bike_data |>
  summarize(
    mean_bikes = mean(bike_count),
    median_bikes = median(bike_count),
    min_bikes = min(bike_count),
    max_bikes = max(bike_count)
  )
```

I also compared bike rentals across seasons, holidays, and functioning days.

```{r}
bike_data |>
  group_by(seasons) |>
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_bikes = mean(bike_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bike_data |>
  group_by(holiday) |>
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_bikes = mean(bike_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bike_data |>
  group_by(functioning_day) |>
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_bikes = mean(bike_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Bike rentals vary across seasons and holidays. Non-functioning hours have zero rentals.

### Removing Non-Functioning Hours

Since the bike rental system was not operating during non-functioning hours, I removed those observations.

```{r}
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  filter(functioning_day == "Yes") |>
  select(-functioning_day)

dim(bike_data)
```

### Creating Daily Data

I combined the hourly observations into daily observations. I used the sum for bike rentals, rainfall, and snowfall, and the mean for other weather variables.

```{r}
bike_daily <- bike_data |>
  group_by(date, seasons, holiday) |>
  summarize(
    bike_count = sum(bike_count),
    rainfall = sum(rainfall),
    snowfall = sum(snowfall),
    temp = mean(temp),
    humidity = mean(humidity),
    wind_speed = mean(wind_speed),
    visibility = mean(visibility),
    dew_point_temp = mean(dew_point_temp),
    solar_radiation = mean(solar_radiation),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(bike_daily)
dim(bike_daily)
```

The daily dataset now has 353 rows and 12 columns.


## Part 3: Exploring Daily Bike Rentals

Now that the hourly data has been combined into daily observations, I looked at how bike rentals vary over time and across different weather conditions.

### Distribution of Daily Bike Rentals

I first used a histogram to look at the distribution of daily bike rentals.

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = bike_count)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Daily Bike Rentals",
    x = "Daily Bike Rentals",
    y = "Number of Days"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Bike Rentals Over Time

I plotted daily bike rentals over time to see how rental activity changes throughout the year.

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = date, y = bike_count)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Bikes Rented"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Bike Rentals by Season

I used boxplots to compare daily bike rentals across seasons.

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = seasons, y = bike_count)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals by Season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Daily Bike Rentals"
  ) +

```

### Bike Rentals by Holiday

I also compared the number of bikes rented on holidays and non-holidays.

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = holiday, y = bike_count)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals by Holiday",
    x = "Holiday",

  ) +

```

### Temperature and Bike Rentals

I created a scatterplot to examine the relationship between average temperature and daily bike rentals.

```{r}
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = temp, y = bike_count)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature vs Daily Bike Rentals",

    y = "Daily Bike Rentals"
  ) +

```

### Correlations Between Numeric Variables

I calculated correlations to see which numeric variables have stronger linear relationships with bike rentals.

```{r}
bike_cor <- bike_daily |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

round(bike_cor, 2)
```

I also looked specifically at the correlations with bike rentals.

```{r}
bike_cor[, "bike_count"] |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)
```

## Part 4: Splitting the Data

Before fitting regression models, I divided the daily dataset into training and testing sets. I used 75% of the data for training and 25% for testing.

I used a stratified split based on seasons so that the different seasons would be represented in both datasets.

### Creating the Training and Testing Sets

```{r}
set.seed(558)

bike_split <- initial_split(
  bike_daily,
  prop = 0.75,
  strata = seasons
)

bike_train <- training(bike_split)
bike_test <- testing(bike_split)
```

### Checking the Split

I checked the number of observations in each dataset.

```{r}
nrow(bike_train)
nrow(bike_test)
```

I also checked the distribution of seasons in the training and testing datasets.

```{r}
bike_train |>
  count(seasons)

bike_test |>
  count(seasons)
```

### Creating a Weekend Variable

Since bike rentals may differ between weekdays and weekends, I created a weekend indicator using the date.

```{r}
bike_train <- bike_train |>
  mutate(
    weekend = factor(
      if_else(wday(date) %in% c(1, 7), "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  )

bike_test <- bike_test |>
  mutate(
    weekend = factor(
      if_else(wday(date) %in% c(1, 7), "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  )
```

### Standardizing Weather Variables

I standardized the numeric weather predictors using the means and standard deviations from the training dataset.

```{r}
weather_vars <- c(
  "temp",
  "humidity",
  "wind_speed",
  "visibility",
  "dew_point_temp",
  "solar_radiation",
  "rainfall",
  "snowfall"
)

train_means <- bike_train |>
  summarise(across(all_of(weather_vars), mean))

train_sds <- bike_train |>
  summarise(across(all_of(weather_vars), sd))

for (v in weather_vars) {
  bike_train[[paste0(v, "_z")]] <-
    (bike_train[[v]] - train_means[[v]]) / train_sds[[v]]

  bike_test[[paste0(v, "_z")]] <-
    (bike_test[[v]] - train_means[[v]]) / train_sds[[v]]
}
```

### Checking Standardized Variables

I checked the standardized temperature variable to confirm that its mean is close to zero and its standard deviation is close to one in the training data.

```{r}
mean(bike_train$temp_z)
sd(bike_train$temp_z)

head(bike_train)
```


## Part 5: Regression Modeling

In this section, I fit three linear regression models to predict daily bike rentals. I compared their performance using root mean squared error (RMSE) on the testing dataset.

### Model 1: Main Effects

The first model includes standardized weather variables, seasons, holiday status and weekend status.

```{r}
model1 <- lm(
  bike_count ~ temp_z + humidity_z + wind_speed_z +
    visibility_z + dew_point_temp_z + solar_radiation_z +
    rainfall_z + snowfall_z + seasons + holiday + weekend,
  data = bike_train
)

summary(model1)
```

### Model 2: Adding Interactions

The second model includes the main effects and interactions between temperature and humidity, temperature and season and holiday and weekend status.

```{r}
model2 <- lm(
  bike_count ~ temp_z + humidity_z + wind_speed_z +
    visibility_z + dew_point_temp_z + solar_radiation_z +
    rainfall_z + snowfall_z + seasons + holiday + weekend +
    temp_z:humidity_z + temp_z:seasons + holiday:weekend,
  data = bike_train
)

summary(model2)
```

### Model 3: Adding Quadratic Terms

The third model includes the interactions from Model 2 and quadratic terms for temperature and humidity.

```{r}
model3 <- lm(
  bike_count ~ temp_z + humidity_z + wind_speed_z +
    visibility_z + dew_point_temp_z + solar_radiation_z +
    rainfall_z + snowfall_z + seasons + holiday + weekend +
    temp_z:humidity_z + temp_z:seasons + holiday:weekend +
    I(temp_z^2) + I(humidity_z^2),
  data = bike_train
)

summary(model3)
```

### Comparing Model Performance

I calculated the RMSE for each model using the testing dataset. A lower RMSE indicates better predictive performance.

```{r}
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}

pred1 <- predict(model1, newdata = bike_test)
pred2 <- predict(model2, newdata = bike_test)
pred3 <- predict(model3, newdata = bike_test)

model_results <- tibble(
  model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
  test_rmse = c(
    rmse(bike_test$bike_count, pred1),
    rmse(bike_test$bike_count, pred2),
    rmse(bike_test$bike_count, pred3)
  )
)

model_results
```

### Selecting the Best Model

I selected the model with the lowest testing RMSE.

```{r}
best_model_name <- model_results |>
  arrange(test_rmse) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(model)

best_model_name
```

### Refitting the Best Model Using All Data

After selecting the best model, I standardized the weather variables using the complete daily dataset and refit the model.

```{r}
bike_full <- bike_daily |>
  mutate(
    weekend = factor(
      if_else(wday(date) %in% c(1, 7), "Weekend", "Weekday")
    )
  )

for (v in weather_vars) {
  bike_full[[paste0(v, "_z")]] <-
    as.numeric(scale(bike_full[[v]]))
}

best_formula <- switch(
  best_model_name,
  "Model 1" = formula(model1),
  "Model 2" = formula(model2),
  "Model 3" = formula(model3)
)

final_model <- lm(best_formula, data = bike_full)

summary(final_model)
```

### Final Model Coefficients

I extracted the coefficients from the final model.

```{r}
final_coefficients <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(final_model)),
  estimate = as.numeric(coef(final_model))
)

final_coefficients
```

### Conclusion

I compared three linear regression models to predict daily bike rentals. Model 1 had a testing RMSE of 4205 while Models 2 and 3 had RMSE values of 2835 and 2833 respectively. Model 3 performed slightly better than Model 2 and had the lowest testing RMSE. I selected Model 3 and refit it using the complete daily dataset. The final model had an adjusted R-squared value of 0.9173.

```{r}
model_results |>
  arrange(test_rmse)
```
